posts.body:
Microsoft kicked off Ignite 2026 on Tuesday, November 17, with a keynote from Satya Nadella, Microsoft's chairman and CEO, and Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft's commercial business. Ignite is Microsoft's yearly conference for the people who build on and run its cloud. I watched the keynote live as a .NET architect with 12 years on Microsoft's stack. It ran about two hours and 45 minutes counting the pre-show, which is long for a keynote, and .NET wasn't mentioned once. My read is neutral, and it wasn't a slam dunk for Microsoft.

Here for the transcript? [Download the full transcript](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/downloads/microsoft-ignite-2026-opening-keynote-transcript.txt) as a text file. It's about 23,600 words with timestamps, and the word counts and a segment index are at the end of this post.

## Four quotes from the keynote

**Can you trust the models?**
Satya Nadella - Chairman and CEO - Microsoft
"How can you even trust all this powerful technology? And the reality is, by definition, you can't."

**Ambition belongs to people**
Judson Althoff - CEO, Commercial Business - Microsoft
"Technology doesn't have ambitions, people do."

**Trust comes from observability**
Judson Althoff - CEO, Commercial Business - Microsoft
"The only way to gain trust is through observability. If you can't observe, manage, govern, secure and measure the value of the AI solutions in your technology environment, you simply can't trust it."

**The token bill**
Mustafa Suleyman - CEO, Microsoft AI - Microsoft
"Right now token spend is going through the roof and at frontier prices. The math just isn't sustainable."

## What Microsoft announced on day one

Microsoft's day-one recap led with six announcements, and three more came up on stage. Here is each one in plain terms, with its status from Microsoft's [Book of News](https://news.microsoft.com/events/ignite/2026/book-of-news/) and where this post covers it.

**Copilot Workspaces** (Frontier customers)
A shared space where people and their agents work toward one goal with shared context. Nadella pitched it as AI moving from single player to multiplayer, and the [workspace pulls in the files and people](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/blog/2026/11/17/copilot-at-microsoft-ignite-expanding-whats-possible-with-intelligence-built-for-work/) a task needs.

**Microsoft IQ** (generally available)
One layer of company context for Copilot and agents, built from Work IQ (Microsoft 365 data), Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, Web IQ and third-party systems, with hundreds of new connectors. Business plugins can be shared and inherited as playbooks.

**New MAI models**
Microsoft Decision 1.1 is generally available, and Nadella said over 4,000 customers have used it, including Epic. [The rest of the list](https://microsoft.ai/news/microsoft-ignite-2026/): Image 2.7 and Image 2.7 Flash in public preview, Realtime 1, Transcribe Dragon, Code 2, Code 2 Flash and Cyber 2 Flash, plus licensed weights for trusted partners. MAI Code 2 is generally available in GitHub, and most of the others are in preview. Code 2 and Cyber 2 Flash come up again in the cost and security sections below.

**Microsoft Perception** (generally available)
[Red, blue and green team security agents](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/perception-blog/whats-new-with-microsoft-perception-at-ignite-2026/4571834) working through playbooks, with a person in control. See "Red, blue and green agents" below.

**Agent 365 Business Analytics** (Frontier preview)
Nadella called it "an ERP system of AI usage." It shows what's driving AI spend, ties that spend to business outcomes, and forecasts cost scenarios so finance can set guardrails and chargebacks. See "The bill got its own segment" below.

**AI Transparency Initiative** (announced)
[Open standards for checking what AI systems see and do](https://news.microsoft.com/source/2026/11/17/microsoft-and-organizations-across-industries-launch-ai-transparency-initiative-to-strengthen-enterprise-trust-in-ai-models-and-agents/), built with more than 40 organizations and applied across Microsoft's MAI models, Foundry and Copilot. See the security section below.

**Autopilot** (rolling out to Frontier customers)
An autonomous agent that, as Nadella described it, keeps moving your work around the clock in the places your team already collaborates. Copilot Code, a no-code app builder in the same release, is in Frontier now with general availability planned for December.

**Salesforce in Copilot, Teams and Fabric**
Microsoft and Salesforce are bringing Salesforce data and actions into Microsoft's tools, a pairing Microsoft calls Copilotforce. The Copilot plugin is in preview and Sales Cloud in Teams is in a pilot. The Fabric data link is already generally available.

**Cobalt 200 virtual machines** (generally available)
Azure VMs on Microsoft's own Cobalt 200 chip, which Nadella called its highest-performance general-purpose VMs. Microsoft claims up to 50% better performance than Cobalt 100 and plans 23 regions by the end of the year. Of everything announced, this is the piece a .NET team could run its existing apps on tomorrow.

## Trust was the theme, the week after an outage

Nadella opened by addressing last week. On Thursday, November 12, a [Microsoft 365 outage](https://aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/13/microsoft-hit-by-global-outages-what-happened-and-why) hit users in 74 countries, taking Outlook down and disrupting Teams and Copilot. He told the room Microsoft has work to do on the resilience customers count on. I respected that he said it first, and it set up the shakiest part of the pitch.

## "Intelligence grounded in trust"

The keynote framed AI as technology that amplifies human ambition and turns "intelligence grounded in trust into real world impact," with trust as one of its pillars. Trust felt like an ironic word to build a keynote on after the year Microsoft has had with its own people. In July, it [cut about 4,800 jobs](https://www.techcrunch.com/2026/07/06/microsoft-lays-off-nearly-5000-employees-across-xbox-commercial-sales), roughly 2.1% of its workforce, after [offering voluntary buyouts to about 9,000 US employees](https://english.aaj.tv/news/amp/330462520) earlier in the year. Nadella made the honest version of the point himself. Alignment and a real understanding of how these models work are still out of reach, so "by definition, you can't" fully trust them. His answer is to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. That's a sound architecture principle, and an admission that the trust problem isn't solved.

## What I didn't hear

Across the whole keynote, Windows got a short passage about running AI models locally on a new generation of PCs, plus a mention as a way to contain agents on devices. .NET, Visual Studio, Azure DevOps and SQL Server got no mention at all, and neither did LinkedIn. .NET did have its own stage a week earlier: [.NET 11 shipped on November 10](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/announcing-dotnet-11/), the day .NET Conf opened. Azure came up mostly as the place the AI runs, with more than 500 data centers across 80 regions. The hardware news was Maia 300 chips for AI and the Cobalt 200 VMs. I didn't hear a roadmap for the Azure and Windows we already build on. As someone who has spent his career on both, that made me a little sad.

Xbox came up once, as an internal customer: the Xbox team uses Microsoft's new decision models to sort player feedback on game launches. There was nothing about gaming itself, four months after Xbox took the hardest hit in July's layoffs, with [1,600 staffers cut that day](https://www.techcrunch.com/2026/07/06/microsoft-lays-off-nearly-5000-employees-across-xbox-commercial-sales).

OpenAI, Microsoft's biggest AI partner for years, came up mainly as a competitor. Althoff said Anthropic and OpenAI now handle documents, slides and spreadsheets with "simplified viewers and editors," while Copilot brings the full Word, Excel and PowerPoint. The rest of the time, OpenAI was one name on a list of model providers, or one of the outside platforms Agent 365 can now manage. The message was clear: Microsoft is going all in on AI, and the core business can wait. That's my read of this keynote and its focus on selling products. .NET 11 had its own launch a week earlier, and the rest of Ignite runs through November 20. Microsoft's [Book of News](https://news.microsoft.com/events/ignite/2026/book-of-news/) also lists Azure SQL updates and a Windows Server 2028 preview. Neither made the keynote.

## The AI platform

Copilot is now pitched as "the new operating system for work," with all of Office built into it and plugins for Dynamics 365 and Salesforce. Althoff went further and said that "anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less." That's a big claim to make from a stage, and one I'd want to test before repeating it. Still, I do see an advantage in Copilot as a productivity tool. In Althoff's demo, it read his inbox and Teams messages, then built a PowerPoint storyboard and an Excel tracker inside the real Office apps. Having all of Office built in, with your email and meetings behind it, is a real head start. What Microsoft still won't share is a paid seat count. Amy Hood, Microsoft's CFO, told analysts last quarter that the company [did not disclose an updated Copilot number](https://uctoday.com/microsoft-ignite-2026-will-copilot-prove-its-value), pointing to revenue and usage instead.

Foundry, Microsoft's platform for building AI apps and agents, now lets you define private benchmarks and evaluations. It measures your agents against them, then improves the agent or the model underneath based on what happens in production. Microsoft also announced licensed weights for its own MAI models, so trusted partners can get the model weights directly. That builds on [Microsoft's June launch of seven MAI models](https://microsoft.ai/news/building-a-hillclimbing-machine-launching-seven-new-mai-models/), when developers could first tune MAI model weights themselves and Frontier Tuning began building custom models on a company's own data. For a company that wants to own its intelligence instead of renting it, that's the most interesting change in the keynote. [One outside analysis](https://the-context.pages.dev/en/news/2026-06-10-mai-frontier-tuning-enterprise-lockin/) points out the trade: the smoother Microsoft makes tuning, the deeper the lock-in.

## The bill got its own segment

A big part of the keynote was about AI cost and the guardrails that keep it from running away. Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, said what he hears from every CIO and CFO is that "token spend is going through the roof and at frontier prices," and that "the math just isn't sustainable." The Copilot demos priced their own work at about $45 in credits for one Cowork session. In the demo, IT had to set a spend limit before anyone could use Copilot Cowork, and users had to ask IT for more once they hit it. Agent 365's new Cost Management, in preview, sets spending limits and alerts per agent or department, including hard caps that stop usage at the limit, and it forecasts spending when an agent's cost spikes. The model pitches followed the same line. Foundry's model router is up to 65% cheaper than sending everything to a frontier model, and MAI Code 2 scores 98% of GPT-6.1 on everyday coding benchmarks for 40% of the cost. Cost is a major concern for every business right now. The days of token maxing, throwing the biggest model and the most tokens at every problem, are ending. I'm glad the guardrails ship with the product, ahead of the first surprise invoice.

## Security tools for a world full of agents

Security got a real share of the stage, and all of it was built around agents. Microsoft said AI models have become very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities over the past year, so this month's Patch Tuesday fixed more than 1,000 of them, compared with fewer than 100 in March. With AI, researchers and attackers alike now find bugs for under $5 that bounty programs pay about $300,000 for. Microsoft also said the window between discovery and exploitation is approaching zero.

Its answer is a new security stack. Defender, Entra, Purview and Sentinel sit underneath as the sensors, and new "actuators" act at machine speed to contain a device or revoke a compromised identity. Microsoft Perception, generally available today, runs on top. It's fed by more than 500 security connectors and what Microsoft says is over 165 trillion signals a day. Every agent gets its own identity in Entra, so admins can govern it like a user, with Agent 365 as the control plane. Microsoft claims the new MAI Cyber 2 Flash model beats OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on the CyberGym benchmark at under 2% of the cost per task. Nadella's best example was Defender containing an autonomous AI attack framework as it tried to move across a network. Microsoft also announced an AI Transparency Initiative for open standards that verify what agents see and do because, in Nadella's words, what a model says about itself "cannot be trusted." Later, Leigh-Ann Russell, chief information officer and global head of engineering at BNY, described a live treasury trade negotiated between a BNY agent and a Microsoft agent. The teams "tested, tested, tested" first. A human watched the whole run with the power to pause or stop it, and a human made the final call on the trade.

### Red, blue and green agents

Perception borrows the way human security teams already work. In security, a red team plays the attacker and a blue team plays the defender, and Microsoft built agents for both. Blue team agents hunt and investigate threats. Red team agents probe your environment the way a skilled penetration tester would, working through a web app's authentication and APIs. They can also use threat intelligence to mimic real attackers. Then Microsoft added a third color. Green team agents, which it called "the fixers," repair your security posture and fix code. You can trigger these agents automatically and manage them as a team, the same way you'd manage a human security staff. Custom playbooks string them together for bigger jobs like threat hunting.

## Software factories, mentioned and dropped

Nadella said software engineering is moving from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts, and that human judgment and expertise still matter. Then he moved on. He said more on [The Pragmatic Engineer podcast](https://www.technologyrecord.com/article/microsoft-ignite-2026-satya-nadella-predicts-rise-of-the-software-factory), recorded before Ignite, where he said "code has gone from being input to output" and that specification and intent matter more now. On stage, there was no word on how a team would actually build or run a factory with Microsoft's tools. That's the part I wanted to hear, because it's close to how I work today.

## GitHub is feeling the agents

Nadella said GitHub is seeing exponential increases in pushes, commits, Actions runs and pull requests, all driven by agents, and that GitHub rebuilt its core to keep up. In testing, Microsoft pointed about 5,000 agents at one repository and sustained 7,200 writes per second, which it put at 180 times today's throughput. Nadella also said GitHub's new Copilot Fusion, which routes each task across Anthropic and OpenAI models, ranks first on Terminal-Bench. That's true for that one test. On [Artificial Analysis's full coding agent index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/github-copilot-fusion-orchestrates-anthropic-and-openai-models-to-balance-performance-and-cost), though, it scores 2 points below Claude Code with Opus 5.5, at about half the cost per task ($5.59 against $11.42). The volume of AI-written code is real. Whether that code is any good is a separate question, and quality is where I spend most of my hours.

## The closest thing to engineering practice

I came for coding news: new programming tools and best practices. The coding news was AI: Copilot Fusion and the MAI Code 2 models. The closest the keynote came to engineering practice was a Foundry demo with Alaska Airlines. Seth Juarez, a principal program manager on Microsoft's AI Platform team, built an agent to tag maintenance reports with the right industry code. His line was the best one for engineers all day: "Just because we made an agent doesn't mean that we know it's working." Foundry graded the agent against a rubric, and its optimizer rewrote the system prompt and tool descriptions until accuracy improved. The longer instructions raised the token bill, so he fine-tuned a smaller MAI Code 2 Flash model to carry those instructions in its weights, and accuracy climbed into the 90s. That measure-then-tune loop is what I'd want on any team shipping AI, and I wish the keynote had spent more time on it.

## HorizonDB is the one I'd watch

The announcement I'd actually try is Azure HorizonDB, a distributed, managed PostgreSQL database with built-in search and AI features. Microsoft aims it at bigger, mission-critical workloads than Azure Database for PostgreSQL, its existing managed Postgres service. HorizonDB entered private preview at Ignite 2025 with a claim of [up to 3 times faster than open-source Postgres](https://siliconangle.com/?p=721481). Nadella said it delivers 8 times the performance of self-managed Postgres and announced it as generally available in Azure. He also said it's coming into Microsoft Fabric, so agents can reason over live transactions and historical data together. [Microsoft prices it per vCore](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/horizondb/), for the primary and its high-availability replicas, with model usage billed through Foundry on the same invoice. Before I'd move a workload, I'd want to know whether 8 times faster is worth the per-vCore price against a well-tuned Postgres I already run.

## The room

The energy in the arena was low, and you could feel it even on the stream. The clapping from the stage was awkward to watch. That matters less than the products, but a keynote is a sales pitch, and this one didn't land in the room the way Microsoft would have wanted.

## Where I land

The keynote felt product-driven more than technology-driven. About three quarters of the stage time, roughly 108 of 145 minutes, went to products and customer stories. The technology came in short bursts: Nadella's architecture point about trust, GitHub's rebuilt core and the Foundry tuning loop. That fits a conference built for IT decision-makers, but it isn't what I came for.

Althoff closed with the two lines I'll remember. The first was "Technology doesn't have ambitions, people do." It's the right thing to say in a keynote that spent most of its time on agents, and it reads differently after a year of layoffs. The second was the line I liked best: "The only way to gain trust is through observability. If you can't observe, manage, govern, secure and measure the value of the AI solutions in your technology environment, you simply can't trust it." I agree with it, and it's a fair standard to hold Microsoft to as well.

For .NET and Azure teams, I'd treat this keynote as a map of where Microsoft's money is going. I'd test HorizonDB and the Foundry evaluation loop on real work before buying into the rest.

**A simple way to remember:**
Trust → measure it before you claim it
Token spend → cap it before the invoice
Your stack → read the .NET 11 release notes
Observability → the bar for every AI tool

What is your team still waiting on from Microsoft that has nothing to do with AI?

## Watch it yourself

The full keynote is on [Microsoft's YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZR4v1c4CClc) if you want to judge it for yourself. You can also [download the full transcript](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/downloads/microsoft-ignite-2026-opening-keynote-transcript.txt) as a text file for your own analysis.

posts.body:
My auction's bidding rules sit in a project with one reference, and it isn't a database.

The site is TheYard, a used-car auction I build in C# and .NET as my portfolio. Claude writes most of its code, and I decide what goes live.

Onion architecture is a way to arrange code in rings. The business rules sit in the middle. The code that carries out what a visitor asks for wraps them. The database code and the web endpoints sit on the outside. One rule holds it together: code may use the rings inside it and never the ones outside it. [Jeffrey Palermo named the pattern](https://jeffreypalermo.com/2008/07/the-onion-architecture-part-1/) on July 29, 2008, with that rule at its center, and [Robert C. Martin's The Clean Architecture](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html), August 13, 2012, calls it the Dependency Rule and calls the database and the web details.

A few words this post uses:

- **Ring**: one layer of the code. In TheYard each inner ring is its own .NET project.
- **Domain**: the business rules, here the auction's: who may bid, how much and when.
- **Port**: an interface the inner code declares for something it needs from outside, such as a place to keep bids.
- **Adapter**: a class in an outer ring that implements a port against one real database.

Slide 2 in the slides below draws TheYard's onion: Data in the middle, then Domain, then Application, with the web endpoints and the database adapters in the outside ring, every arrow pointing inward, and Azure SQL and Cosmos DB outside the onion altogether. The full drawing, with every project named, is on the site's [rings diagram page](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/api/docs/diagrams/rings).

Slide 3 defines each ring, from the middle out:

- **Data** (textbook: the domain model's records): plain records with no behavior and no dependencies, which every ring may read. In TheYard: `Vehicle` and `PhotoEntry`.
- **Domain** (textbook: the domain model's rules): the business rules as pure functions. The same inputs give the same answer, and the clock is handed in. In TheYard: `BidRules` and `AuctionSchedule`.
- **Application** (textbook: use cases): the use cases, which run the rules in the right order, and the ports, which are interfaces for what the middle needs from outside. In TheYard: `PlaceBidHandler` and `IBidStore`.
- **Outside ring** (textbook: infrastructure and UI): the web endpoints read a request and ask Application, and the adapters implement the ports against one real database each. In TheYard: `EfBidStore` and `CosmosBidStore`.

The databases themselves, Azure SQL and Cosmos DB, sit outside the onion. Palermo's 2008 post says it directly: the database is not the center, it is external.

In October I walked through [TheYard's rings one at a time](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7516149383609114626/). This post is about the point under all of them: the rules in the middle know nothing about the database or the web. Here are five lessons on keeping it that way, written so you can use them in your own project tomorrow. Every count was read from the code at release 1.0.5.55.

## 1. Point every dependency inward

The auction's rules are the part of TheYard that must not break. A bid that goes through when it should be refused costs a real buyer money, and I didn't want those rules tied to a database driver or a web framework.

So the rules live in their own project, Domain, in the middle. Its [project file](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Domain/TheYard.Domain.csproj) has one reference, to the Data project that holds the plain vehicle shapes, and no NuGet package at all:

`<ProjectReference Include="..\TheYard.Data\TheYard.Data.csproj" />`

That is the whole trick, and the compiler enforces it for free. Code in Domain that reaches for Entity Framework, the Cosmos DB SDK or ASP.NET doesn't compile, because the project can't see them. Domain holds 24 C# files today, and the rule for a bid is [one static method](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Domain/Shared/Auction/BidRules.cs#L67) that takes a vehicle, an amount, a clock and whether the car is sold, and answers with an outcome.

## 2. Hand the rules the clock

Every auction on TheYard opens and closes at set times. A rule that reads `DateTime.UtcNow` for itself gives a different answer every time it runs, so a test of it can only ask what happens "now".

I needed tests that could name an exact moment: one millisecond before an auction opens, the moment it opens, the last millisecond before it closes and the moment it closes.

So the rules never read the clock. [`BidRules`](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Domain/Shared/Auction/BidRules.cs) and [`AuctionSchedule`](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Domain/Shared/Auction/AuctionSchedule.cs#L50) take the time as an argument, and the web layer reads the server's clock and hands it in. The build backs it up: one of the architecture tests reads every method in Domain for a call to the system clock and fails on the first one it finds.

The result is [a test](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Tests/AuctionScheduleTests.cs#L42-L57) that checks those four exact milliseconds with no database, no web server and no waiting. With a rule that read the clock for itself, that test could not be written.

## 3. Put the database behind a port

TheYard runs on two very different databases: Azure SQL, through Entity Framework Core, and Cosmos DB, through its own SDK. The same rules have to save a bid to either one without knowing which.

The answer is dependency inversion, the D in SOLID. The inner ring declares the interface it needs, in its own words, and the outer ring implements it. Application declares [`IBidStore`](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Application/Shared/Auction/Ports.cs#L43). [`EfBidStore`](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Infrastructure/Shared/Auction/EfSources.cs#L56) implements it for Azure SQL, [`CosmosBidStore`](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Infrastructure.Cosmos/Shared/Auction/CosmosSources.cs#L53) for Cosmos DB, and `MemoryBidStore` for the tests. The one place that names a real adapter is [the wiring at startup](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Api/Shared/Wiring/StoreRegistration.cs#L160). Name the port for what the middle needs, `IBidStore`, and keep the technology out of the name. `ISqlBidRepository` would leak it.

To be plain about what this did and did not do: when Cosmos DB arrived, the port itself had to change once. Every method became a `Task`, because the Cosmos DB SDK has no way to answer without waiting on the network. That touched every caller one time. After it, the Cosmos DB adapters arrived as new classes and no bid rule changed. [Microsoft's .NET architecture guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures), updated March 7, 2023, describes the same move and the same payoff: because the core doesn't depend on infrastructure, it is easy to unit test.

## 4. Let a test hold the rings, then test it

A rule that only code review holds slips the first busy week, and I didn't want to be the person who has to remember it. So I gave the rule to the build.

[`OnionTests`](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/api/TheYard.Tests/OnionTests.cs) uses NetArchTest, a library that opens the compiled .NET code and checks which types use which. Reading compiled code matters, because it sees inside method bodies and lambdas, so a dependency hidden in a handler fails as surely as a `using` line would.

It started with ten rules in early October, and I watched each one fail before I trusted it. Four failed on their first run against my own code: the endpoint rules found handlers reaching into the service container and composing the bid services themselves, the Cosmos DB rule found that adapter borrowing a type from the SQL one, and the database rule found three queries written in the web project, one hidden in a lambda. I fixed each, then proved the other six by planting a forbidden reference and watching the build go red.

Then the tests had a gap of their own, and it was mine. On October 21 a review planted six violations, one per ring: a vehicle shape with a rule and a file read inside it, a Domain class starting a process, an adapter with a second buy-now rule, and more. Every architecture test passed with all six in. The rules allowed the whole `System` namespace in every ring, so they only caught what they named. In release 1.0.4.24 I tightened them until each planted file failed by name. The file holds 19 rules today.

I know I'm not alone here. Anyone who has trusted a green test that checked less than its name says hits this one. The fix is the same as for any test: make it fail on purpose before you believe it.

## 5. Slice the onion by feature

The rings held, but a feature like bidding was spread across folders named for kinds of code: the endpoint in one, the wiring in another, the handler in a third, and about 90 files loose at the root of the web project. To change bidding you opened four folders and guessed which files mattered.

On October 20, in release 1.0.4.0, every feature became one folder with one name, used in every ring that holds its code. `Features/Bids` in the web project holds the endpoint and a `Module` that wires it; `Features/Bids` in Application holds the handlers. The rules and the database code that bidding shares with the vehicle pages sit in a `Shared` folder in each ring, and a test fails the build when one feature reaches into another. The web project has ten feature folders and 13 modules today, and `Program.cs` finds the modules itself, so it stays at 56 lines and a new feature adds no line to it.

[Jimmy Bogard's Vertical Slice Architecture](https://www.jimmybogard.com/vertical-slice-architecture/), April 19, 2018, is where the idea comes from: couple along a slice, not across a layer. Bogard builds slices instead of layers. TheYard keeps the rings and cuts the slices through them, because the rings are what let the database change without touching the rules. The full decision is [ADR-107: The onion cut into vertical slices](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/docs/decisions/ADR-107-the-onion-cut-into-vertical-slices.md).

## When not to build it this way

The rings cost projects, interfaces and tests, and they pay that back only when there is something to protect. TheYard has two databases behind the same rules and rules worth testing on their own, so the cost is worth it here.

A small service over one table is clearer as one project, with Entity Framework called from the endpoint. A spike written to learn something fast is one file. A script that reads, changes and writes needs no layers at all. Add a ring the day a second database or a rule worth testing alone shows up. The middle road is folders: The Shed, a file browser that lives beside TheYard, is one project with its rings as folders, held by the same kind of tests by namespace.

## More from the same rings

- **CQRS sits inside them.** My post [CQRS for beginners](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?view=blog&post=cqrs-for-beginners) splits every request into a query or a command, and its handlers sit in the same feature folders.
- **The full record.** [ADR-088: Onion and SOLID](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/4a56b44a4b51772243bb6a3bbd839b61f98b7bae/docs/decisions/ADR-088-onion-and-solid.md) lists every ring, what is kept on purpose and every addendum since October 3.
- **The practices page.** [Onion architecture, the practices](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=onion) follows one bid through the rings with the live code, and shows how to make a rule go red on your own repository in five steps.

A simple way to remember:

- Dependencies → point inward
- Clock → handed in
- Database → behind a port
- Rings → held by a test
- Feature → one folder per ring

What would have to change before you split a small service into rings?

## References

- [The Onion Architecture: part 1, Jeffrey Palermo, July 29, 2008](https://jeffreypalermo.com/2008/07/the-onion-architecture-part-1/)
- [The Clean Architecture, Robert C. Martin, August 13, 2012](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2012/08/13/the-clean-architecture.html)
- [Common web application architectures, .NET architecture guides, Microsoft Learn, updated March 7, 2023](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/modern-web-apps-azure/common-web-application-architectures)
- [Vertical Slice Architecture, Jimmy Bogard, April 19, 2018](https://www.jimmybogard.com/vertical-slice-architecture/)
- [NetArchTest.eNhancedEdition, the library the architecture tests use](https://github.com/NeVeSpl/NetArchTest.eNhancedEdition)

the database code and the web endpoints sit on the outside. one rule holds it together: code may use the rings inside it and never the ones outside it. jeffrey palermo named the pattern on july 29, 2008, with that rule at its center, and robert c. martin's the clean architecture, august 13, 2012, calls it the dependency rule and calls the database and the web details. a few words this post uses: - ring : one layer of the code. in theyard each inner ring is its own .net project. - domain : the business rules, here the auction's: who may bid, how much and when. - port : an interface the inner code declares for something it needs from outside, such as a place to keep bids. - adapter : a class in an outer ring that implements a port against one real database. slide 2 in the slides below draws theyard's onion: data in the middle, then domain, then application, with the web endpoints and the database adapters in the outside ring, every arrow pointing inward, and azure sql and cosmos db outside the onion altogether. the full drawing, with every project named, is on the site's rings diagram page. slide 3 defines each ring, from the middle out: - data (textbook: the domain model's records): plain records with no behavior and no dependencies, which every ring may read. in theyard: vehicle and photoentry . - domain (textbook: the domain model's rules): the business rules as pure functions. the same inputs give the same answer, and the clock is handed in. in theyard: bidrules and auctionschedule . - application (textbook: use cases): the use cases, which run the rules in the right order, and the ports, which are interfaces for what the middle needs from outside. in theyard: placebidhandler and ibidstore . - outside ring (textbook: infrastructure and ui): the web endpoints read a request and ask application, and the adapters implement the ports against one real database each. in theyard: efbidstore and cosmosbidstore . the databases themselves, azure sql and cosmos db, sit outside the onion. palermo's 2008 post says it directly: the database is not the center, it is external. in october i walked through theyard's rings one at a time. this post is about the point under all of them: the rules in the middle know nothing about the database or the web. here are five lessons on keeping it that way, written so you can use them in your own project tomorrow. every count was read from the code at release 1.0.5.55. 1. point every dependency inward the auction's rules are the part of theyard that must not break. a bid that goes through when it should be refused costs a real buyer money, and i didn't want those rules tied to a database driver or a web framework. so the rules live in their own project, domain, in the middle. its project file has one reference, to the data project that holds the plain vehicle shapes, and no nuget package at all: <projectreference include="..\theyard.data\theyard.data.csproj" / that is the whole trick, and the compiler enforces it for free. code in domain that reaches for entity framework, the cosmos db sdk or asp.net doesn't compile, because the project can't see them. domain holds 24 c files today, and the rule for a bid is one static method that takes a vehicle, an amount, a clock and whether the car is sold, and answers with an outcome. 2. hand the rules the clock every auction on theyard opens and closes at set times. a rule that reads datetime.utcnow for itself gives a different answer every time it runs, so a test of it can only ask what happens "now". i needed tests that could name an exact moment: one millisecond before an auction opens, the moment it opens, the last millisecond before it closes and the moment it closes. so the rules never read the clock. bidrules and auctionschedule take the time as an argument, and the web layer reads the server's clock and hands it in. the build backs it up: one of the architecture tests reads every method in domain for a call to the system clock and fails on the first one it finds. the result is a test that checks those four exact milliseconds with no database, no web server and no waiting. with a rule that read the clock for itself, that test could not be written. 3. put the database behind a port theyard runs on two very different databases: azure sql, through entity framework core, and cosmos db, through its own sdk. the same rules have to save a bid to either one without knowing which. the answer is dependency inversion, the d in solid. the inner ring declares the interface it needs, in its own words, and the outer ring implements it. application declares ibidstore . efbidstore implements it for azure sql, cosmosbidstore for cosmos db, and memorybidstore for the tests. the one place that names a real adapter is the wiring at startup. name the port for what the middle needs, ibidstore , and keep the technology out of the name. isqlbidrepository would leak it. to be plain about what this did and did not do: when cosmos db arrived, the port itself had to change once. every method became a task , because the cosmos db sdk has no way to answer without waiting on the network. that touched every caller one time. after it, the cosmos db adapters arrived as new classes and no bid rule changed. microsoft's .net architecture guide, updated march 7, 2023, describes the same move and the same payoff: because the core doesn't depend on infrastructure, it is easy to unit test. 4. let a test hold the rings, then test it a rule that only code review holds slips the first busy week, and i didn't want to be the person who has to remember it. so i gave the rule to the build. oniontests uses netarchtest, a library that opens the compiled .net code and checks which types use which. reading compiled code matters, because it sees inside method bodies and lambdas, so a dependency hidden in a handler fails as surely as a using line would. it started with ten rules in early october, and i watched each one fail before i trusted it. four failed on their first run against my own code: the endpoint rules found handlers reaching into the service container and composing the bid services themselves, the cosmos db rule found that adapter borrowing a type from the sql one, and the database rule found three queries written in the web project, one hidden in a lambda. i fixed each, then proved the other six by planting a forbidden reference and watching the build go red. then the tests had a gap of their own, and it was mine. on october 21 a review planted six violations, one per ring: a vehicle shape with a rule and a file read inside it, a domain class starting a process, an adapter with a second buy-now rule, and more. every architecture test passed with all six in. the rules allowed the whole system namespace in every ring, so they only caught what they named. in release 1.0.4.24 i tightened them until each planted file failed by name. the file holds 19 rules today. i know i'm not alone here. anyone who has trusted a green test that checked less than its name says hits this one. the fix is the same as for any test: make it fail on purpose before you believe it. 5. slice the onion by feature the rings held, but a feature like bidding was spread across folders named for kinds of code: the endpoint in one, the wiring in another, the handler in a third, and about 90 files loose at ring that holds its code. features/bids in the web project holds the endpoint and a module that wires it; features/bids in application holds the handlers. the rules and the database code that bidding shares with the vehicle pages sit in a shared folder in each ring, and a test fails the build when one feature reaches into another. the web project has ten feature folders and 13 modules today, and program.cs finds the modules itself, so it stays at 56 lines and a new feature adds no line to it. jimmy bogard's vertical slice architecture, april 19, 2018, is where the idea comes from: couple the rules. the full decision is adr-107: the onion cut into vertical slices. when not to build it this way the rings cost projects, interfaces and tests, and they pay that back only when there is something to protect. theyard has two databases behind the same rules and rules worth testing on their own, so the cost is worth it here. a small service over one table is clearer as one project, with entity framework called from the endpoint. a spike written to learn something fast is one file. a script that reads, changes and writes needs no layers at all. add a ring the day a second database or a rule worth testing alone shows up. the middle road is folders: the shed, a file browser that lives beside theyard, is one project with its rings as folders, held by the same kind of tests by namespace. more from the same rings - cqrs sits inside them. my post cqrs for beginners splits every request into a query or a command, and its handlers sit in the same feature folders. - the full record. adr-088: onion and solid lists every ring, what is kept on purpose and every addendum since october 3. - the practices page. onion architecture, the practices follows one bid through the rings with the live code, and shows how to make a rule go red on your own repository in five steps. a simple way to remember: - dependencies → point inward - clock → handed in - database → behind a port - posts.title: CQRS for beginners: is it a question or a change?
posts.summary: My site has 67 kinds of request, and one word in each name says if it can change anything. Five lessons from moving TheYard to partial CQRS: the code is split, the database is not.

images.alt_text: Title slide: CQRS for beginners. TheYard uses partial CQRS: the code is split, reads and writes share one database. 3 services and 27 handlers before; 0 services, 67 handlers now.

posts.body:
My site has 67 kinds of request, and one word in each name says if it can change anything.

The site is TheYard, a used-car auction I build in C# and .NET as my portfolio. Claude writes most of its code, and I decide what goes live.

CQRS stands for command query responsibility segregation. It sounds harder than it is. Every request a program answers either asks a question or asks for something to change. Asking which cars are for sale is a question. Placing a bid is a change. CQRS means you write those two kinds of request as two kinds of code:

- **A query** asks a question. It reads and changes nothing.
- **A command** asks for a change. It may answer with what it did.
- **A handler** is the one class that answers one request.

TheYard uses **partial CQRS**. The code is split into queries and commands, but both read and write the same database. There is no separate read database, no events copying data from one side to the other and no event sourcing. Section 5 explains why.

The site has 45 queries, 22 commands and 67 handlers, and not one class named Service. Those counts come from the site's [CQRS practices page](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=cqrs), and a test checks them against the code on every build, so they cannot drift. Here are five lessons from the change that got it there on October 23, 2026, written so you can use them in your own project tomorrow.

## 1. Let the name say what the code can do

Before the change, TheYard had 27 handlers, and none of their requests said what kind of request they were. They had loose names like `PlaceBid`, `VehicleSearch` and `BlogOpen`. To learn whether a piece of code could change anything, you had to open it and read it.

I wanted one word to answer that question for every request on the site.

In release 1.0.4.39 every request became a small record named for what it does, ending in `Query` when it reads and `Command` when it changes something. Each one got exactly one handler, named the same with `Handler` in place of the last word. The whole mechanism is two C# interfaces in [Requests.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Application/Shared/Requests.cs), `IQueryHandler` and `ICommandHandler`, with no library between a route and the code it runs.

Here are two real ones from the blog you are reading now, in [BlogHandlers.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Application/Features/Blog/BlogHandlers.cs#L35-L46):

`public sealed record ReadPostQuery(string Slug);`
`public sealed record SavePostCommand(BlogPost Post);`

`ReadPostQuery` opens this post. `SavePostCommand` saves one, and only the site's operator can send it. You can tell which is which from the name, before you open the file.

## 2. Give a question read-only access

The blog stored its posts behind one interface, `IBlogStore`, which carried the reads and the writes together. So the query that lists the blog's posts was handed `SaveAsync`, the method that saves one. Nothing used it that way, but nothing stopped a later change from using it. That was my design.

A question should not be able to change anything, even by mistake, so the fix had to take the write away from the query rather than trust everyone to leave it alone.

I split the interface in two in [BlogStore.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Application/Features/Blog/BlogStore.cs#L15-L46). `IBlogReader` holds the reads. `IBlogStore` extends it and adds the three writes:

`public interface IBlogReader { ... }`
`public interface IBlogStore : IBlogReader { Task<int> SaveAsync(...); ... }`

Every query now takes `IBlogReader`, and only the commands take `IBlogStore`. The same split went into the accounts and the link tracking. The query that lists posts has no way to save a post, whatever someone types into it later.

That is the payoff of the split. A query can only read, and a command is the only path to a write, so reads and writes don't leak into each other, and a whole kind of bug is ruled out before anyone writes it.

If this looks familiar, it is the I in SOLID, interface segregation. CQRS turned it from a habit into a rule.

## 3. Split the service that does everything

`BidService` had grown to 502 lines across four files. It placed bids, reset them and read the standings. Beside it sat `InventoryService` in five files and `MarketService`, which runs the simulated auction room, and a class called `Auction` held all three. Every bid handler and every vehicle handler took `Auction`, so any read on the site could reach every write the three services had.

I needed each job to stand on its own, so a read could only reach reads.

Each job became its own handler. The shared data the handlers need became three parts in [AuctionParts.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Application/Shared/Auction/AuctionParts.cs), the stock, the bids and the room, each with a reading interface and a writing interface. The catalog query [SearchVehiclesHandler](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Application/Features/Vehicles/VehicleHandlers.cs) takes the reading side only. The bid command [PlaceBidHandler](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Application/Features/Bids/PlaceBidHandler.cs) reads the vehicle the same way, then writes through `IBidWriter` and nothing else.

`Auction` and the three services are gone, and nothing in that code is named Service today. The change touched 121 files, wide and shallow: mostly renames.

I know I'm not alone here. Anyone who has opened a 500-line service class knows this one.

## 4. Let a test hold the rule

Nobody should have to remember the rule. I wanted the build to catch a broken one before a reviewer had to.

[CqrsTests.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/api/TheYard.Tests/CqrsTests.cs) holds six checks, and each reads the compiled C# on every build:

- every handler is exactly one query handler or one command handler, named for its request
- every query and every command has exactly one handler, and is handled as what its name says
- a query handler is handed no store and no writer
- a query handler is handed nothing with a method that starts with Save, Write, Delete, Add, Remove or a similar verb, whatever the interface is called
- no class in that code is named Service
- the counts on the practices page match the code

The tests went red on the old code before the change, which proved they could fail. Two days later, on October 25, I tightened the fourth check to read what an interface can do instead of trusting its name. To prove it, I planted one write method on a reader interface, and the build went red at once with the handler's name and the method it could reach.

## 5. Split the code, not the database

The CQRS articles I found first spent their time on separate read and write databases, events that keep the two in step, and event sourcing. I had to decide how much of that TheYard needs.

I started with the people who wrote about it first. [Martin Fowler's CQRS article](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html), July 14, 2011, warns that the full pattern adds risky complexity to most systems and belongs in the parts that need it. [Microsoft's CQRS pattern page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs), updated February 21, 2025, calls one shared database the basic form and lists what separate stores cost: keeping them in step, and reads that can be behind the writes. [Greg Young's CQRS Documents](https://cqrs.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/11/cqrs_documents.pdf) trace the idea to Bertrand Meyer's command-query separation and treat event sourcing as a good pairing but an optional one.

So TheYard stops at partial CQRS: the queries and the commands read and write the same database. The site does run two databases, Azure SQL and Cosmos DB, but that is a different choice. Neither one is a read copy of the other, and each serves the queries and the commands for its own data, with no queue or bus between a read side and a write side. A bid's new price has to be readable by the buyer the moment it lands, and a second store for reads would put that at risk for a speed the site does not need. If a read ever gets too slow for the store that holds the writes, that is the day to add a second one.

## More from the same change

- **Opening a page can be a command.** When you open a blog post, the site keeps a count of the read. That makes the request a command, `RecordReadCommand`, even though it feels like a read. Name a request by what it does, not by what it feels like.
- **No mediator library.** I looked at MediatR and a hand-written dispatcher and kept neither. Each feature maps its route straight to its handler, so "go to definition" on a route lands on the code that runs.
- **The rest followed the same evening.** The 24 reads behind the site's admin pages became 21 queries and 3 commands in release 1.0.4.43.
- **It sits inside two earlier rules.** CQRS here is one rule inside the site's onion layers and its vertical slices: [the onion and SOLID](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=adr-onion-and-solid) and [the onion cut into vertical slices](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=adr-the-onion-cut-into-vertical-slices). [Jimmy Bogard's Vertical Slice Architecture](https://www.jimmybogard.com/vertical-slice-architecture/), April 19, 2018, makes the same point: organize code by request, and each request is already a command or a query.

The full decision, with what was weighed and what was left out, is [ADR-115: A request is a query or a command](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/fab5f9ebfc5a9a8442d33750dc690f1ef25d356f/docs/decisions/ADR-115-a-request-is-a-query-or-a-command.md).

A simple way to remember:

- Name → Query or Command
- Question → read-only access
- Big service → one handler per job
- Rule → a test holds it
- Database → one, for reads and writes

Which class in your code can change data when it only needs to read it?

## References

- [CQRS, Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com, July 14, 2011](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html)
- [Command Query Separation, Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com, December 5, 2005](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CommandQuerySeparation.html)
- [CQRS pattern, Azure Architecture Center, Microsoft Learn, updated February 21, 2025](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs)
- [CQRS Documents, Greg Young, uploaded November 2010](https://cqrs.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/11/cqrs_documents.pdf)
- [Vertical Slice Architecture, Jimmy Bogard, April 19, 2018](https://www.jimmybogard.com/vertical-slice-architecture/)
- [CQRS, the practices, TheYard, read November 16, 2026 at release 1.0.5.52](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=cqrs)

Lesson 2: Count everything that's stored. Bars: deploy 169.4 MB in 8 packages, blog 8.4 MB in 68 pictures, the other two 6 KB.
Lesson 3: Check the meter against the bill. The live card's egress dial at 82.08 GB of the free 100 GB.
Lesson 4: Give the first answer a second pass. Claude's first answer beside the second pass that read the query.
Lesson 5: Prove the cause with one read. The infrastructure file puts the app and its storage in the same region.

posts.body:
My cloud dashboard warned I'd used 82 GB of my free 100 GB this month, from storage that holds 0.18 GB.

TheYard is the website I build to show employers how I work. It runs on Azure, Microsoft's cloud, where I rent storage and computing by the month instead of owning servers. Claude, an AI assistant, writes most of the code, and I decide what is allowed to go live.

The site has a [dashboard](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?view=admin) with a dial for each Azure service it uses, like the gauges in a car. A dial turns amber when something needs a look and red when something is wrong.

On Thursday, November 12, 2026, the dial for Blob Storage turned amber. Blob Storage is where the site keeps its pictures and the code for my job-hunt app. The dial read 82.08 GB of data sent out this month, and Microsoft lets every account send the first 100 GB a month out free, then charges by the gigabyte. Azure calls that outgoing data egress. The dial goes amber at 80 GB.

That morning taught me five things about reading a dial before acting on it.

## 1. Read the query behind the dial

The dial's card listed 8.4 MB stored, the size of my blog's pictures. The first answer I got from Claude that morning took that number as everything in Blob Storage, reasoned that 8.4 MB of pictures could not produce 82 GB, and blamed the shared drive that lives in the same storage account.

Before anything changed, I needed to know what the dial actually counted. So I read its query, the code that fetches its number. [Line 113 of StorageSource.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/35ba9575b876fc1d061449f65c8dc800b52989fc/api/TheYard.Api/Features/Admin/Cloud/StorageSource.cs#L113) builds the address of the blob service alone, and [line 138](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/35ba9575b876fc1d061449f65c8dc800b52989fc/api/TheYard.Api/Features/Admin/Cloud/StorageSource.cs#L138) reads Azure Monitor's Egress metric on that address.

So all 82 GB came from Blob Storage.

## 2. Count everything that's stored

My own first instinct, before I knew any of this, was to compress every image and PDF in storage. That would have been real work on a guess.

Instead I listed what Blob Storage holds. The card's own "Kept" line says 177.8 MB in 111 files, split across four containers:

- **deploy:** 169.4 MB in 8 files, the code packages for my job-hunt app on Azure Functions
- **blog:** 8.4 MB in 68 files, the blog's pictures, already compressed as WebP
- **the two Azure Functions housekeeping containers:** 6 KB between them

The card's 8.4 MB showed the smallest real container and left out the biggest. Compressing 8.4 MB of pictures could not explain 82 GB, so the cleanup that matters for this dial keeps only the newest two code packages. I still approved lossless compression for everything stored, run nightly, as housekeeping against bloat.

## 3. Check the meter against the bill

The dial grades blob egress against Azure's free 100 GB, which is a line on the bill. I wanted to know whether the meter and the bill measure the same thing, so I read Microsoft's own pages on November 12, 2026.

The [Azure Blob Storage monitoring reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/blobs/monitor-blob-storage-reference) says the Egress metric counts data sent to outside clients and data sent within Azure, and that it does not reflect billable egress. The [Azure bandwidth pricing page](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/bandwidth/) says data moving between Azure services in one region is not charged.

So the dial held a number that can include free traffic up against a line on the bill.

## 4. Give the first answer a second pass

Claude's first answer was confident, and I let it go into the written instructions for two Claude agents: one to dig through the shared drive and one to change the cards.

Before either agent started, a second pass read the query behind the dial. It found the blob service address on line 113, and both sets of instructions went on hold with nothing changed.

That is how I work with Claude: small steps I can check, each one proved before the next. A wrong first answer costs a few minutes that way, not a morning of compressing the wrong files.

I know I'm not alone here. Anyone doing AI development hits this one.

## 5. Prove the cause with one read

The likely reader is my job-hunt app itself. It runs on Azure Functions Flex Consumption, which starts new copies of the app as work arrives, and Microsoft's [Flex Consumption page](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-functions/flex-consumption-plan) says the app gets its package from a blob container on startup. My [infrastructure file](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/35ba9575b876fc1d061449f65c8dc800b52989fc/infra/jobhunt.bicep#L24) puts the app and its storage in the same region, centralus, and [lines 193 and 194](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/35ba9575b876fc1d061449f65c8dc800b52989fc/infra/jobhunt.bicep#L193-L194) point the app's deployment at the deploy container. The card's own read chart leaves out reads the Functions host makes with the account key, which is why the reads looked quiet while egress climbed.

That is a strong guess, and it is still a guess. Before changing anything, I'm adding one read to a GitHub Actions workflow, [azure-read.yml](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/35ba9575b876fc1d061449f65c8dc800b52989fc/.github/workflows/azure-read.yml), that splits blob egress by hour and by caller, and it runs once.

Once it confirms the cause, the dial grades blob egress against its own normal for the past week instead of the free 100 GB, the card calls the number blob egress, and the deploy container keeps its newest two packages.

## The same storage account, three weeks earlier

This storage account has taught me something before. In October the shared drive in it ran up a one-day bill because every folder listing on a file share is billed, which I wrote up as [a $25 day from an Azure file share](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?view=blog&post=a-25-dollar-day-from-a-file-share).

A simple way to remember:

- Dial → read the query behind it
- Storage → count all of it
- Meter → check it against the bill
- First answer → give it a second pass
- Cause → prove it with one read

What's one dashboard number your team trusts without reading the query behind it?

## References

- [Azure Blob Storage monitoring data reference, Microsoft Learn, read November 12, 2026](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/blobs/monitor-blob-storage-reference)
- [Bandwidth pricing, Microsoft Azure, read November 12, 2026](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/bandwidth/)
- [Azure Functions Flex Consumption plan hosting, Microsoft Learn, updated October 30, 2026](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-functions/flex-consumption-plan)

- [The blob service card, TheYard Admin tab, read 08:50 CST November 12, 2026](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?view=admin&card=blob)

posts.title: Lee Markum Told Me to Blog. Here's Why You Should Too.
posts.summary: A thank-you to my friend Lee Markum, the SQL Server blogger who pushed me to start writing, and a nudge for any professional who has never written about their work.

posts.body:
I'm a team lead and .NET architect, and for most of my career the problems I solved stayed inside the teams I solved them for. My friend Lee Markum changed that. This post is a thank-you to Lee and a nudge for any working professional who has never written a word about their work.

## The conversation that started it

During my job search, Lee and I were talking regularly. He suggested I start blogging and sharing what I know, as a way to add authenticity to the search. Then he said something that stuck with me: "Steve, we have these conversations and you have so much to offer the community. You don't realize it. I'm hearing what problems you're solving, but no one else knows." So I started writing. I now publish posts on LinkedIn and keep a copy of each one here on my own site, TheYard. Has it helped the job search? A little, and I'll be honest about that, because the reason to start goes beyond any one search.

## Who Lee is

Lee has worked with SQL Server since 2009, and his site, [leemarkum.com](https://leemarkum.com/), is built around helping teams get more out of it: faster queries, better uptime and environments that are easier to run. That alone would make him worth following. What makes him a great member of the tech community is everything he does on top of it.

He has been blogging since 2015, sharing what he learns for free. In 2022 he [spoke at the PASS Data Community Summit](https://leemarkum.com/archive/2022/12/speaking-at-the-pass-data-community-summit/), which he calls the world's largest SQL Server conference, presenting a live stream while attending in person. He has also spoken at SQL Saturday and DevUp, and on November 17, 2026 he's presenting Query Store to the Orange County Microsoft Fabric + SQL User Group, in person in Irvine and online. He takes part in T-SQL Tuesday, the monthly event where SQL Server bloggers all write on one shared topic. He keeps a free [SQL Server installation and learning guide on GitHub](https://github.com/lmarkum/Resources). And his writing goes past databases: career development is his second-largest category, with posts on mentoring and leadership.

He also does the thing that never shows up on a resume. He reposts people who are looking for work so their posts reach his network. When a friend is job hunting, he sends leads. One lead Lee sent me turned into a recruiter email within days of my applying.

## What we have in common

- **Hunter Engineering.** We both worked there, and our time overlapped in 2018.
- **SQL Server.** Lee lives in it. I spent years tuning one that powered a live financial advisory platform.
- **Azure.** He moved his blog to Azure Static Web Apps this October. My site runs on Azure too.
- **Linux Mint home labs.** He's building a SQL Server 2025 lab on a Linux Mint host. My old gaming PC is now my Linux Mint home server, and Lee reposted my post about it.
- **Coaching.** He writes about mentoring, and my favorite part of leading a team is coaching the next generation of engineers.

## Why you should start

Lee answered the big question himself this week in [Is Blogging Still Relevant in 2026](https://leemarkum.com/archive/2026/11/is-blogging-still-relevant-in-2026/). His case: a blog is an easier place to start than video, and the writing skills you need already came with your education. I'd add one thing from my side. Your coworkers see a ticket close. A blog post shows how you thought about the problem, and that record is yours no matter where you work next.

If you stopped writing years ago, Lee shows you can pick it back up. He blogged steadily from 2015, slowed down after 2022, and came back this October with a [new site on Hugo and Azure](https://leemarkum.com/archive/2026/10/goodbye-wordpress-how-i-migrated-to-hugo-and-azure-static-web-apps/) and six posts in under a month.

## How to start this week

Pick one problem you solved recently. Write it for someone with no context: what broke and how you fixed it. A few hundred words is plenty. Publish it anywhere, and LinkedIn counts.

## Go read Lee

Start with [Is Blogging Still Relevant in 2026](https://leemarkum.com/archive/2026/11/is-blogging-still-relevant-in-2026/). If you work anywhere near a database, his [SQL Server 2025 lab on Linux series](https://leemarkum.com/archive/2026/10/building-a-sql-server-2025-lab-on-linux-part1/) is worth a bookmark. You can also connect with him on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leemarkum/).

Lee, thank you for the push, and for seeing something in my work before I did.

So here's my question for you: what did you fix this month that someone else is still stuck on? Write that one down.

## References

- Lee Markum, [leemarkum.com](https://leemarkum.com/)

posts.title: AI's instinct was to escalate. Mine was to look.
posts.summary: Claude makes me about twice as productive, but it doesn't replace judgment. One failed email lookup, a support email I never sent, and four lessons on using AI without depending on it.

images.alt_text: Title slide: Hunter.io finds a person's work email from their name and company; every call failed with restricted_account until one login fixed it in about a minute.
Lesson 1 of 3, Know when to ask for help and when to dig: ten minutes in Claude drafted a support email; deep research showed 50 of 50 searches unused.
Lesson 2 of 3, Look at the source before you escalate: Claude's next step was a support email, Steven's was to open a tab and log in.
Lesson 3 of 3, Own the part you built: the automation ran for days without anyone checking the Hunter account; Claude drafts, Steven makes the call.
Sources slide: Hunter's help center on restricted accounts, Hunter's account FAQs, and Anthropic's Building effective agents guide.
Using AI without depending on it: about twice as productive by Steven's estimate, and the judgment and ownership stay with him.

posts.body:
For days, every email lookup my job-hunt automation made failed, and one login fixed it in about a minute.

My job hunt runs on automation that Claude operates for me on Azure Functions and a Linux server in my house. An online application usually goes through an automated filter before a person ever sees it, so after each application I write directly to the engineering leader who runs that team. Company websites name those leaders but rarely list their email addresses. That is the gap Hunter.io fills: it is a service that finds a person's work email address from their name and company, and my automation calls it once for each leader.

On November 11 and 12, 2026, I learned that every one of those lookups had been failing. Each call came back with the same error, restricted_account, and the automation had found zero addresses. Fixing it took one login, and it taught me three things about working with AI.

Claude makes me about twice as productive on research and basic coding. That is my estimate, not a measurement: I know I wouldn't have automated this much of my job hunt, or built out TheYard, my portfolio site, this far without it. This morning was a reminder of the part it doesn't replace.

## 1. Know when to ask for help and when to dig

Every Hunter call was failing, and I needed to find out why. About ten minutes in, after one web search, Claude's answer was to hand the problem to Hunter's support team, and it drafted the email for me to send. AI is good at producing the next piece of work, like a draft or an email.

Part of a Staff engineer's job is knowing when to ask for help and when to dig. Before anything went out, I had to decide whether an email was the right move at all, so I sent Claude back to do deep research first. Claude did the research; my part was deciding it was needed.

That research found the account had been restricted from its very first call. The dashboard still showed all 50 of its searches unused. It also read the error text past the code, restricted_account, and the text said to log in to Hunter for more information. Hunter's help center lists the common reasons an account gets [restricted or blocked](https://help.hunter.io/en/articles/1893956-why-has-my-account-been-blocked-or-restricted-for-suspicious-behavior), and its [account FAQs](https://help.hunter.io/en/articles/15654553-hunter-account-faqs) say Hunter may ask a new account to verify a phone number. The error itself pointed somewhere faster than either page: the login.

## 2. Look at the source before you escalate

Claude still wanted to send the support email. My instinct was to see the account for myself.

I skipped the email, opened a browser tab and logged in to Hunter. Hunter showed a pending account-setup step.

About a minute after I logged in, the API worked. Two leader addresses came back that same morning, and the support email was never needed.

## 3. Own the part you built

I built this automation, and it ran for days without anyone checking the Hunter account itself. The answer sat on a dashboard I had never opened. That miss is mine.

My view of AI is that it makes mistakes the way a person does, including on this one: it went straight to the next artifact instead of asking whether the artifact was needed. So I run it the way I would run a capable teammate. Claude drafts, I make the call, and I move from one small step I can check to the next, so a mistake gets caught before it is sent or built on.

This time the check at the source cost me about a minute.

## Using AI without depending on it

This part is my opinion, not a study: what worries me is how fast developers, senior and junior, are learning to hand AI their judgment along with their typing. The tools are a real breakthrough, and the speed is worth having. The risk is that the next artifact starts to feel like the answer, because it arrives so quickly and reads so well.

This morning I could have sent the email Claude drafted ten minutes in. A Staff engineer knows when to ask for help and when to dig. I dug in, and that choice is the part AI doesn't replace: the judgment and ownership that come from years of building systems.
