posts.title: Quality on both ends: what my tests and CodeRabbit taught me
posts.summary: My tests grew 3.5 times since September and still finish in about seven minutes. Five lessons from two weeks of a test gate on one end and CodeRabbit on the other.

images.alt_text: Title slide: Quality on both ends. TheYard, my .NET and Azure platform built with Claude, checked by an automated test gate and by CodeRabbit. 1,487 tests in 7.0 minutes on September 21, 5,154 tests in 6.9 minutes at the median on November 11.
Lesson 1 of 5, Give the diagnosis an owner: the fix was written down October 19 and unscheduled, a full run hit 19 minutes, and one Claude agent brought the median from 14.8 minutes to 6.9.
Lesson 2 of 5, Make the rules agree: two instructions disagreed, so the Claude agents ran every test on every change until both lines matched.
Lesson 3 of 5, Watch the gate fail before you trust it: a test broken on purpose in every part of the gate turned every part red, and CodeRabbit flagged exactly the three forbidden changes.
Lesson 4 of 5, Let CodeRabbit stop a release: 22 releases reviewed, 27 findings, none Critical, 16 fixed.
Lesson 5 of 5, Check Claude like you'd check a person: four mistakes in one evening, all caught before the live site.
Others have measured the same pressure: the 2024 DORA report, GitClear's study via DevClass, James Shore's ten-minute build, and Google's mutation testing in code review.
A simple way to remember: Diagnosis, give it an owner. Rules, make them agree. Gate, watch it fail first. CodeRabbit, let it stop a release. Claude, check it like a person.

posts.body:
My site runs 3.5 times as many automated tests as it did in September, and they still finish in about seven minutes.

The site is TheYard, a working .NET and Azure platform I build as my portfolio. Claude writes most of the code, and I decide what is allowed to go live. Every change passes two checks before it reaches the live site:

- **An automated test gate.** It runs all 5,154 tests and blocks any change where a single test fails.
- **An AI code reviewer.** CodeRabbit reads each change the way a teammate reviews a pull request and reports anything that breaks my coding standards.

Two weeks of running both taught me five things. The live numbers behind each one are on the site's [Quality page](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=quality).

## 1. Give the diagnosis an owner

On September 21 a full test run took 417 seconds for 1,487 tests. As the test count grew, so did the wait. On October 19 a run took 825 seconds, and my design notes already explained why: every group of tests ran one after another on a single machine, and splitting the work across two machines would bring it near 520 seconds. I hadn't scheduled that fix.

By November 10 a full run took 1,148 seconds, about 19 minutes, and the same explanation had been written a second time. That afternoon I made the fix my priority and gave the job to one Claude agent with nothing else on its list. The tests now run in five groups side by side, and the slowest group, the browser tests, runs in two halves, the way [Playwright's sharding](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding) is designed to work. Over the ten releases before the change, a full run took 14.8 minutes at the median. Over the fifteen since, it takes 6.9.

James Shore's [ten-minute build](https://www.jamesshore.com/Agile-Book/ten_minute_build.html) rule from The Art of Agile Development is the bar I hold it to.

## 2. Make the rules agree

My Claude agents work from a written instruction file. One line said to leave the slow tests for the final check before release. Another line said to run every test before saving any change. The Claude agents ran everything, every time, because two instructions that disagree get resolved toward more work.

I rewrote both lines to say the same thing: run the tests your change touches, and the final check runs everything.

I know I'm not alone here. Anyone doing AI development or running an LLM software factory hits this one.

## 3. Watch the gate fail before you trust it

A test gate that shows green proves nothing until you have seen it catch something. Before I trusted the new five-part gate, I broke a test on purpose in every part of it and watched every part go red. A second trial failed once on purpose and passed when run again, to prove a retry reads the right result.

I tested CodeRabbit the same way. I gave it six test changes: three that my coding rules allow and three that they forbid. It stayed quiet on the three allowed changes and flagged exactly the three forbidden ones.

Google built the same idea into its own code reviews. Its [mutation testing work](https://research.google/pubs/practical-mutation-testing-at-scale-a-view-from-google/), published in IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering in 2021, changes a developer's new code on purpose to see whether the tests notice, inside a code review system used by more than 24,000 developers.

## 4. Let CodeRabbit stop a release

At first CodeRabbit could only comment. I set it up that way on purpose, so I could see what it reports before giving it any power. This week I decided that a finding it rates Critical will stop the release. Every release already waits for its review, about 10.5 minutes at the median, so the rule adds no extra wait.

Across 22 releases it has raised 27 findings: 2 Major, 21 Minor, 4 Trivial and no Critical yet. 16 of them are fixed, and 2 were answered as wrong with the reason written down.

Before it could block anything, its rules had to match my written coding standards. On November 10 only 1 of its 7 rules did. One rule would have flagged 727 test methods for a standard meant only for production code. All 7 rules now quote my standards word for word, and an automated test fails if they drift apart again.

## 5. Check Claude like you'd check a person

In one evening the Claude agents made four mistakes a person could make:

- slipped an unwanted file into a change, caught by reading the list of changed files
- wrote a test that shut down its own terminal, caught when the terminal closed
- took a release number another Claude agent had already reserved, caught before release
- skipped a build step, caught when the automated checks went red

My checks caught all four before anything reached the live site.

## Why both ends

Google's [2024 DORA report](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report), published October 22, 2024, found delivery stability dropped an estimated 7.2% as AI adoption rose. GitClear's study of 211 million lines of code, [covered by DevClass](https://www.devclass.com/ai-ml/2025/02/20/ai-is-eroding-code-quality-states-new-in-depth-report/1626250) on February 20, 2025, found 2024 was the first year that copy-pasted lines outnumbered moved lines, a sign of less cleanup and more duplication. Those findings are why I check the code on both ends.

## More from the same two weeks

- **Check the passes too.** A second review that worked out every result again found a reviewer rule marked as matching my standards that did not. A review that only rereads the failures inherits the first reviewer's blind spot.
- **Know what your number measures.** The site's published test time ran until the release step, and the release step waits for CodeRabbit. Once the tests got faster, that number was really CodeRabbit's time, so the site now shows the two separately.
- **A new tool brings work nobody ordered.** Every release now opens a pull request for CodeRabbit, and on November 10 those pull requests sent me 29 emails in one day.
- **Reserve the release number at the last moment.** One release passed every test and was still refused, because a number reserved hours earlier by another Claude agent had not been released yet.
- **A wait that reads nothing looks like waiting.** One Claude agent's progress check failed on every read and looked exactly like a slow job. Every wait now prints each read with its time.
- **Count the whole cost of the faster tool.** A local database emulator ran the tests in 106 seconds against 154 on the real cloud database, but it adds about 30 seconds to start and needs an access key into a database built to use none. I did not adopt it.

A simple way to remember:

- Diagnosis → give it an owner
- Rules → make them agree
- Gate → watch it fail first
- CodeRabbit → let it stop a release
- Claude → check it like a person

What stops a bad AI-written change from reaching production on your team?

## References

- [Announcing the 2024 DORA report, Nathen Harvey and Derek DeBellis, Google Cloud blog, October 22, 2024](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report)
- [AI is eroding code quality states new in-depth report, Tim Anderson, DevClass, February 20, 2025](https://www.devclass.com/ai-ml/2025/02/20/ai-is-eroding-code-quality-states-new-in-depth-report/1626250)
- [Ten-Minute Build, James Shore, The Art of Agile Development, July 29, 2010](https://www.jamesshore.com/Agile-Book/ten_minute_build.html)
- [Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google, Goran Petrovic, Gordon Fraser, Marko Ivanković and René Just, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, 2021](https://research.google/pubs/practical-mutation-testing-at-scale-a-view-from-google/)
- [Sharding, Playwright documentation, read November 11, 2026](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding)
- [TheYard Quality page, read November 11, 2026](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=quality)

posts.title: I plan with Claude Fable and let other sessions write the code
posts.summary: I draft the spec with Claude Fable, separate Opus sessions build from it, and the tests decide when a step is done. Four rules every handoff follows, and why small steps matter.

images.alt_text: Title slide: I plan with Claude Fable, other sessions write the code. Me as the architect, Fable as the drafter, Opus building from the prompt file, and tests deciding when it is done.
Rule 1 of 4, questions up front: the coding session writes its own plan and asks every question in one message, then builds without stopping.
Rule 2 of 4, a checklist after every step: re-read the step, confirm no feature was dropped, and run the tests before the next step.
Rule 3 of 4, the gate decides: tests passing and CI green on main close a step, never the session's own report.
Rule 4 of 4, a note for the next session: a DONE note and a NEXT file so the next session reads a file instead of my memory.
The disclaimer: AI makes mistakes just like a human, so I move one small, verifiable prototype at a time and catch mistakes before they are hard to reverse.
Others put the spec first too: Anthropic's Claude Code best practices, GitHub Spec Kit, Microsoft for Developers and Birgitta Böckeler on martinfowler.com.
A simple way to remember: Fable drafts it, the prompt file writes it down, Opus builds it, tests prove it, and small steps catch it early.

posts.body:
Most of my AI time goes into the spec, and Claude Fable is where I draft it.

On my platform, TheYard, I split the work the way I would on a team. I'm the architect and Fable is the drafter, so we go back and forth on the design until the spec is something I'd sign. I like to watch it think, so I start every Fable session myself. Then the spec becomes a prompt file for a separate Claude Code session on Opus, and I move on to the next design while it builds.

Anthropic's [Claude Code best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) recommend the same split: once the spec is complete, start a fresh session to build it, so the new session works from clean context and a written spec.

## How a handoff works

**Questions up front.** The coding session writes its own plan from the spec and asks every question in one message before it starts. Once I answer, it builds without stopping to check in.

**A checklist after every step.** Long runs drift and features get dropped, so every prompt carries a checklist the session reruns after each step.

**The gate decides.** Nothing counts as done until the tests pass and CI on main is green.

**A note for the next session.** Every run ends with a DONE note and a NEXT file, so the next session picks up from a file instead of from my memory.

## AI makes mistakes, just like a human

Even with this method, a session can drop a feature or misread the spec. That's why I highly recommend moving from one small, verifiable prototype to the next. Each step is small enough that I can check the output myself, so I keep control and catch a mistake before it's released or ingrained in the system, where it's hard to reverse.

## Others put the spec first too

GitHub open-sourced [Spec Kit](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/spec-driven-development-with-ai-get-started-with-a-new-open-source-toolkit/) on September 2, 2025, and it breaks the work into four phases that start with the spec and end with the implementation. On September 15, 2025, Den Delimarsky [wrote on Microsoft for Developers](https://developer.microsoft.com/blog/spec-driven-development-spec-kit/) that writing the decisions down first surfaces wrong assumptions while changing course is still cheap. Birgitta Böckeler's [October 15, 2025 look at three spec-driven tools](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/sdd-3-tools.html) on martinfowler.com adds a fair caution: each tool still defines a spec in its own way.

## The job has changed

Being a software lead or Staff engineer has changed dramatically now that AI does the typing. My day goes to design and review, and with close to 20 sessions running, the written spec keeps every one of them pointed the same way.

A simple way to remember:

- Fable → draft it
- Prompt file → write it down
- Opus → build it
- Tests → prove it
- Small steps → catch it early

How do you split planning and coding when you work with AI?

## References

- [Best practices for Claude Code, Anthropic, read November 9, 2026](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)
- [Spec-driven development with AI: Get started with a new open source toolkit, Den Delimarsky, GitHub blog, September 2, 2025](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/spec-driven-development-with-ai-get-started-with-a-new-open-source-toolkit/)
- [Spec-driven development with Spec Kit, Den Delimarsky, Microsoft for Developers, September 15, 2025](https://developer.microsoft.com/blog/spec-driven-development-spec-kit/)
- [Understanding Spec-Driven-Development: Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl, Birgitta Böckeler, martinfowler.com, October 15, 2025](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/sdd-3-tools.html)

posts.title: My resume came back as a job
posts.summary: Seven minutes after I emailed a recruiter, two job descriptions came back quoting my own email. Four tells, and the articles showing this is a known resume-rewrite play.

images.alt_text: Title slide: My resume came back as a job. A timeline from the recruiter's first email to two job descriptions and a request for my resume for initial benchmark.
Tell 1 of 4, my proof line: what I wrote beside what the job description said, four applications and release cycle time cut in half.
Tell 2 of 4, my own sentence: Platform consolidation is the work I enjoy most, quoted back in the job description seven minutes later.
Tell 3 of 4, four company names: a free Gmail address, four companies across two emails, and a greeting with a blank where my name belonged.
Tell 4 of 4, reverse recruiting: the job seeker pays, and the only ask was my resume for initial benchmark.
Others have reported the same play: $100 to $500 CV packages, $499 ATS fixes, about $500 rewrites, and employment scam losses up from $90 million to $501 million.

posts.body:
Until the morning of November 5, 2026, I didn't know a fake recruiter could build a job description out of my own email.

On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, a recruiter emailed me about a remote Staff .NET role. On the morning of November 5 I sent my five standard questions and one proof line: at Storee Construction I consolidated four applications onto one .NET platform on Azure and cut release cycle time 50%.

Seven minutes later I had two job descriptions, salary ranges to the dollar, a named decision-maker on each, and a request for my resume "for initial benchmark."

## What gave it away

**My proof line.** The first role's mandate was to consolidate "four distinct legacy applications" onto Azure, cut release cycle time in half, and mentor a team of four. That was my Storee line, down to the size of the team I led there.

**My own sentence.** The second role said "We know that platform consolidation and improving CI/CD pipelines are the work you enjoy most." I had written "Platform consolidation is the work I enjoy most" seven minutes earlier.

**Four company names.** Two emails named four different companies, all sent from a free Gmail address. The follow-up opened with "Hi ," and a blank where my name belonged, the mark of a mail-merge template.

## Others have reported the same play

In March 2026 [The Irish Times](https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/03/06/an-irish-job-hunter-a-linkedin-post-and-a-fake-recruiter-scam/) told the story of a senior leader who heard from a "recruiter" on a Gmail address within hours of his open-to-work post. The pitch was tailored to his background, his CV then "scored" too low, and a "specialist" quoted CV packages from $100 to $500. The job did not exist.

Career coach [Joanne Meehl wrote up the "your resume needs to be ATS compliant" version](https://joannemeehlcareerservices.com/ezine/Beware-the-fake-job__your-resume-needs-to-be-ATS-compliant%21_%20scam.html) in June 2024, with $499 to fix the resume and $129 for a cover letter. Kelli Hrivnak [walked through the same pattern](https://kellihriv.substack.com/p/no-you-should-not-pay-for-a-resume) in March 2026, where the rewrite cost about $500.

Arthur Lazarus, [writing on KevinMD in March 2026](https://kevinmd.com/2026/03/how-to-spot-artificial-intelligence-recruiters-who-target-candidates-from-linkedin.html), lists being referred to someone who will write a more professional CV at your expense as one step in a fake recruiter's progression. He also suspects the LinkedIn-based outreach he received was written with AI.

The scale keeps growing. - Your words in the job → Written for you
- Answers in minutes → A script
- Candidate pays → You are the customer
- Resume benchmark → The upsell

posts.title: My Linux server runs on one Ethernet cable and an HDMI dummy plug
posts.summary: My old gaming PC is now a Linux server I drive entirely from my laptop screen. Four pieces made it work, from a dummy plug to a shared clipboard.

images.alt_text: Title slide: My Linux server runs on one Ethernet cable and an HDMI dummy plug, driven entirely from a laptop screen.
The Linux Mint System Monitor on WickedAwsome: four CPU cores near 50 percent, 8.4 GB of 33.6 GB memory in use and zero swap.
Step 1 of 4: an Ethernet cable and an HDMI dummy plug, which makes the box render a real 1920x1080 desktop with no monitor.
Step 2 of 4: Tailscale, a private VPN tunnel from the laptop to the server with no ports opened to the internet.
Step 3 of 4: Sunshine streams the Linux Mint desktop to Moonlight on the laptop.
Step 4 of 4: KDE Connect shares the clipboard both ways, so right-click copy and paste works between laptop and server.
A simple way to remember: Ethernet is the network, the dummy plug is a real desktop, Moonlight is the screen and KDE Connect is the clipboard.

posts.body:
An Ethernet cable and an HDMI dummy plug are the only two things plugged into my Linux server besides power.

My old gaming PC is now my first Linux server, WickedAwsome. Its job is to take builds and AI coding sessions off my laptop so the laptop never gets locked up waiting on a long run. You can run a laptop as a server, but that's like hauling a yacht with a Volkswagen Beetle: you can, but you shouldn't. On November 4, 2026 I finished the part that makes it usable: I drive the whole server from my laptop screen and never sit in front of it.

## What it took

**Ethernet and an HDMI dummy plug.** The dummy plug tells the box a monitor is attached, so it renders a real 1920x1080 desktop with no screen on the desk.

**Tailscale.** My first VPN tunnel, set up with [Claude](https://claude.ai)'s help. [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) lets the laptop reach the server privately without a single port opened to the internet.

**Sunshine and Moonlight.** [Sunshine](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine) streams the full Linux Mint desktop, and [Moonlight](https://moonlight-stream.org) shows it on my laptop, smooth enough that I forget it's remote.

**KDE Connect for the clipboard.** Moonlight has no clipboard sync yet. Right-click copy and paste is a key part of how I work. [KDE Connect](https://kdeconnect.kde.org) shares the clipboard both ways, so I copy on the laptop and right-click paste on the server.

## Why I'd encourage you to try Linux

I'd encourage more developers to give Linux a real try. It isn't for everyone, and I'm still polishing this setup, but an old PC and a free OS gave me a second machine that does real work without tying up the one I carry.

A simple way to remember the setup:

- Ethernet → the network
- Dummy plug → a real desktop
- Moonlight → the screen
- KDE Connect → the clipboard

What would it take to get you to try Linux?

posts.title: Scammers read the job market too
posts.summary: A recruiter email that fit my search perfectly failed three of five checks before I opened it. The five checks, and what each one catches.

images.alt_text: A mock of the phishing email: a free Gmail sender, a Re: subject line and a View the email button.
Check 1 of 5: check the sender's domain, because a free inbox is not a search firm.
Check 2 of 5: find the earlier thread behind any Re: subject line.
Check 3 of 5: a message locked behind Gmail confidential mode is a warning sign.
Check 4 of 5: find the role on the employer's own careers page.
Check 5 of 5: never pay a fee or share a Social Security number to apply.
Four lines to remember the checks, and the FTC count of over 105,000 job scam reports in 2024.

posts.body:
**A recruiter email that fits your search perfectly is the one to slow down on.**

At 7:50 AM on October 29, 2026, an email titled "Confidential Leadership Search" arrived in my inbox. The role was Lead .NET Engineer, paying $140K to $180K+. It read like it was written off my resume. Honestly, it surprised me how close it came: the title and the level matched my search. I didn't open it.

Email is only one door. My mom got a call that showed up as Charter, with a local Missouri number. A trusted name and a hometown area code. Caller ID can be faked as easily as an email sender's name, so hang up and call back on the number from the company's own website.

Scammers know the market is rough. They know job seekers check email before coffee, and they write the message that person has been waiting for. According to the [Federal Trade Commission](https://search.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2025/09/ftc-takes-steps-stop-deceptive-unfair-labor-market-practices), job scam reports topped 105,000 in 2024, close to triple the 2020 count, and reported losses passed $513 million.

Here are the five checks I run before I reply to an opportunity. The slides below walk the same five, one per slide. Mine failed the first three.

## 1. Check the sender's domain

Retained search firms and in-house recruiters send from the company's own domain. A free inbox costs a scammer nothing and disappears when it gets reported.

In my inbox: the sender was a free Gmail address running a "confidential leadership search."

## 2. Find the thread behind "Re:"

A subject that opens with "Re:" implies an earlier conversation. Search your inbox for it. A fake reply lowers your guard because it looks like a thread you already trust.

In my inbox: no earlier message from that sender existed.

## 3. Treat a locked message as a warning

[Gmail confidential mode](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7674059) has honest uses, but it also keeps the real content away from spam filters until you click "View the email." A cold recruiter has no reason to hide a job description.

In my inbox: the whole message sat behind that button.

## 4. Find the role on the careers page

Emails and job board listings can be faked. The employer's own careers page is much harder to fake. If the role is not there, ask the recruiter for the requisition number and check again before you send anything.

## 5. Never pay or share your SSN to apply

Background check fees, equipment you buy up front, a crypto deposit to release "earnings" and "direct deposit setup" forms before an offer are the payoff of the scam. A real employer collects your Social Security number after an offer, through its own HR system.

## A simple way to remember

- A free inbox → Not a search firm
- A "Re:" with no thread → A setup
- A locked message → A filter dodge
- Pay or SSN first → Walk away

If something fails, report it. In the Gmail app, open the message, tap the three dots and choose Report phishing. You can also file at [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov).

Stay vigilant. The email or call you've been waiting on may not be the breakthrough it looks like. A real recruiter will still be there after two minutes of checking.

What red flags have you caught in your own search?

## References

- Federal Trade Commission, [FTC takes steps to stop deceptive and unfair labor market practices](https://search.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2025/09/ftc-takes-steps-stop-deceptive-unfair-labor-market-practices), Business Guidance Blog, September 24, 2025
- Google Gmail Help, [Send & open confidential emails](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/7674059)
- [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov)
- [TheYard on GitHub](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard)

It also takes the heavy work off my laptop. Builds and AI coding sessions run on the server, so the laptop stays light for what I do on it every day, and nothing slows down while a long run finishes.

- .NET runs natively on Linux, the same OS most cloud containers run on, so what I test at home looks like what runs in production.

- Docker, SSH and scripting are built in.
- It's free, so the only cost is the hardware I already own.

posts.title: $25 a day for an Azure file share?
posts.summary: A cloud file share bills you for looking, not for storing: the four-day, $25-a-day spike, why the card missed it, and what changed.

images.alt_text: Title slide: $25 a day for an Azure file share? A cloud file share bills you for looking, not for storing.

Bar chart of one Azure subscription's daily cost from Sep 27 to Oct 25, 2026: under $1.32 a day until Oct 19, then $3.07, $7.82, $13.41 and $24.99 on Oct 20 to 23 while the share was listed 50 million times, then $2.00 and $1.71 after the sync was unregistered.

What happened: a sync task, a mounted drive that forgot its folder listings every 30 seconds, and an editor's file watcher drove 50 million requests in four days, 88 percent of them checks of a file's details.
Why I missed it for four days: the forecast read $60.58 while the month was at $70.20, nobody read the day rows, and a $735 a month projection on a phone was the alarm.

What changed: stopped the looking, changed the price plan to Transaction optimized, fixed the forecast to start from spend, put an alarm on the meter at 20,000 requests an hour and a $50 budget, gave the share its own card, and read the day-by-day rows before any summary.
A simple way to remember: storage is cheap and looking is not, a forecast is a summary and the rows are the truth, the fix for a surprise bill is an alert on the meter.
Closing slide: what is the meter on your bill that nobody is watching? Mine was a file share; the gigabytes were never the bill.

posts.body:
𝗔 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Last week my Azure bill went from $1.32 a day to $24.99 a day in four days. The chart on slide two is the real one, off my own Admin tab.

Nothing grew. The share held the same gigabytes the whole time. What changed was how many times something looked at it.

𝟭. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱
I had moved a working folder into an Azure Files share so an Azure Function could run my job hunt without my laptop. The share was on the Hot tier, which bills every request: every time anything lists a folder, checks a file's details or writes to it.

Then the laptop that mounted it kept looking. A sync task walked the whole folder. The mounted drive's folder listings expired every 30 seconds. My editor watched the mounted folder for changes. Over four days that came to 50 million requests, 88 percent of them checks of a file's details.

𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗜 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀
My cost card showed a forecast, and the forecast was built from Azure's own projection, which runs two days behind. The day rows had the answer on day one. Nobody read the rows. I found out from a $735 a month projection on my phone.

𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱
→ Stopped the looking. The sync job that re-read the whole folder is gone. The drive now remembers a folder listing for an hour instead of 30 seconds, so it asks the cloud once instead of 120 times. My editor no longer watches that folder.
→ Changed the price plan. Azure Files has three tiers: Hot charges little to store and a lot per request, and Transaction optimized is the reverse. My folder is small and touched constantly, so the cheaper-per-request tier wins.
→ Fixed the forecast. It used to repeat Azure's own projection, which runs two days behind. Now it takes what has been spent and adds the rest of the month at yesterday's rate, so a bad day shows the next morning.
→ Put an alarm on the meter. Azure emails me if the share gets over 20,000 requests in an hour, about three times a quiet hour, and again when the month passes 80 percent of a $50 budget.
→ Gave the share its own card. My site's Admin page shows the share's requests this hour against the alarm line, and who is making them, so a walker shows up while it is still walking.
→ Changed the review habit. Every look at the bill reads the day-by-day rows before any summary; a day over twice the usual gets flagged.

The day after the fix the row read $2.00. The day after that, $1.71.

𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿:
→ Storage is cheap. Looking is not.
→ A forecast is a summary. The rows are the truth.
→ The fix for a surprise bill is an alert on the meter, not a better guess.

The full postmortem, with a source on every number, is on my site. Links in my first comment.

What is the meter on your bill that nobody is watching?

Save this for the next time a "cheap" resource surprises you.

posts.title: The spec has to run
posts.summary: AI beats most developers at typing code and loses to good ones at judgment. Five steps to AI code you can trust, each on a real TheYard file.

images.alt_text: Title slide: five steps to AI code you can trust, Dave Farley's rules shown on a real file from TheYard.
Step 1, write the spec first: the whole spec is one test name saying the cloud merger leaves the same bytes as the laptop merger.
Step 2, watch it go red: the parity test compares the two mergers' output byte for byte.
Step 3, let the agent make it green: the TrackerMerger class talks to the IMergeStore port and knows nothing of the share.
Step 4, keep the spec out of reach: the CI workflow runs the Function's tests on a clean GitHub runner on every push to main.
Step 5, small steps: the merger stays idle until its MERGER setting is on, so the hand-over was one setting.
A summary slide pairing each step with a short phrase, ending with: the spec has to run.

posts.body:
**AI beats most developers at typing code, and loses to good ones at judgment.**

The bet on replacing engineers is the wrong bet. My own multiplier with AI is about 1.5x, and none of it came from the tool.

On October 21, Dave Farley put out a video on his Modern Software Engineering channel, [I Said This Years Ago: Why Prompting AI Code Fails (And What Works)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EkH_uoybj8k), that says why. AI changed the cost of one activity, producing code. It did nothing for the hard problems around it: saying what you want, proving you got it, moving in small steps.

The same week, the merger behind my job-search tracker moved from a PowerShell script on my laptop to C# in Azure, with AI drafting the code against tests I wrote first. Here are his five steps, each one tied to a real file in [TheYard](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard). The slides below walk the same five, one file per slide.

## 1. Write the spec first

One scenario, in the language of the problem, before the agent starts. Say what the system must do, not how.

In TheYard: the whole spec is one test name, `The_cloud_merger_leaves_the_same_bytes_as_the_laptop_merger`, in [ParityTests.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/functions/jobhunt.Tests/ParityTests.cs).

## 2. Watch it go red

Red is the proof that your spec can catch a wrong answer. A test written after the code only proves the code does what it already does.

In TheYard: `Assert.Equal` on the master file, the moved-out file and every spool folder. 1,743,354 bytes and 79,903 bytes, identical.

## 3. Let the agent make it green

The agent owns the how. Read its code when the risk warrants it, not because every line demands it.

In TheYard: the rules talk to a port, `IMergeStore`. Nothing in them knows the share exists.

## 4. Keep the spec out of reach

The tests are the contract. A change to one is a change to the contract, and a person approves it.

In TheYard: every push to main runs the Function's tests on a clean GitHub runner.

## 5. Small steps

One scenario: red, green, review, commit. Small steps are how you find out you are wrong while it is still cheap to be wrong.

In TheYard: the same five input files ran on Azure in a scratch folder first and gave the same SHA-256, the file's fingerprint. Then the hand-over was one setting, `MERGER=on`. The numbers are in the [decision record](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=adr-the-tracker-merger-runs-in-azure).

## A simple way to remember

- Say what, not how → Specify
- Make it fail before it passes → Verify
- Let the agent own the how → Green
- Tests are the contract → Protect them
- One scenario at a time → Small steps

Farley's point that stuck with me: the agent can draft the tests, and a person who understands the problem decides which ones count. That part is the job.

Who on your team writes the check that proves the code did what was asked?

## References

- Dave Farley, [I Said This Years Ago: Why Prompting AI Code Fails (And What Works)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EkH_uoybj8k), Modern Software Engineering on YouTube, October 21, 2026
- [Dave Farley on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dave-farley-a67927/)
- [The parity test, ParityTests.cs](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/functions/jobhunt.Tests/ParityTests.cs)
- [The decision record, ADR 111: The tracker merger runs in Azure](https://theyard.stevenstout.biz/?doc=adr-the-tracker-merger-runs-in-azure)
- [The LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7519090977731633152/)
- [TheYard on GitHub](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard)

posts.title: SOLID in five real files
posts.summary: All five SOLID principles in five small files of The Shed, a .NET 10 file browser: the rule in plain words, then the real file that follows it.

images.alt_text: Title slide: SOLID, shown in real .NET code, five rules each shown on a real file from The Shed.
Single Responsibility: FileBrowser asks NamePattern what matches and SearchMatches when to stop, and only puts the answer together.
Open/Closed: a new kind of error is one more line in ApiRefusalException, and one handler turns every error into a clean response.
Liskov Substitution: PhysicalFileStore and the test's FakeStore both implement IFileStore and swap in without the rules noticing.
Interface Segregation: the IFileStore interface lists only what the rules need from a disk, children, descendants, read and move.
Dependency Inversion: FileBrowser takes an IFileStore, and only the wiring in FilesRegistration names the real disk.
A summary slide pairing each SOLID letter with a short phrase to remember it by.

posts.body:
**You can see all five SOLID principles in five small files.**

SOLID is five rules that keep code easy to change. The names are hard to recite. The habits are easy to spot once you know where to look.

Here they are in [The Shed](https://theshed.stevenstout.biz), a small file browser I built in .NET 10 for people learning the stack. Each principle gets the rule in plain words, then the real file that follows it. The slides below walk the same five, one per principle.

## 1. Single Responsibility (SRP)

A class should have one job and one reason to change.

In The Shed: [FileBrowser](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Application/FileBrowser.cs) runs the search. [NamePattern](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Domain/NamePattern.cs) decides what matches. [SearchMatches](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Domain/SearchMatches.cs) decides when to stop. Three jobs, three classes.

## 2. Open/Closed (OCP)

Open for extension, closed for modification. Add new behavior without rewriting what already works.

In The Shed: a new kind of refusal is one new line in [ApiRefusalException](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Application/ApiRefusalException.cs). No existing class changes.

## 3. Liskov Substitution (LSP)

Anything that implements an interface must be swappable for any other implementation without breaking the caller.

In The Shed: the tests swap [FakeStore](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/tests/TestProject.Tests/SampleTree.cs) in for [PhysicalFileStore](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Infrastructure/PhysicalFileStore.cs). FileBrowser never notices.

## 4. Interface Segregation (ISP)

No class should depend on methods it does not use. Small, specific interfaces beat one big general one.

In The Shed: [IFileStore](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Application/IFileStore.cs) has ten methods, every one a file or folder operation. No web, no config, no logging leaks in.

## 5. Dependency Inversion (DIP)

High-level code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete implementations.

In The Shed: FileBrowser takes `IFileStore`, the interface. The one line that knows about the real disk is in the [wiring](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/blob/main/samples/theshed/Composition/FilesRegistration.cs).

## Why it matters

- Lower coupling → a change stays where you made it
- Higher testability → each piece tests on its own
- Easier maintenance → clear ownership, fewer bugs, fewer merge conflicts

## A simple way to remember

- One job per class → S
- Add a line, not a rewrite → O
- Swap the real for the fake → L
- Ask for only what you need → I
- Depend on the interface → D

The names matter less than the habit. Code can follow all five before you can recite them.

Which of the five do you catch yourself breaking most often?

## References

- [The Shed, live](https://theshed.stevenstout.biz)
- [The Shed's code, samples/theshed on GitHub](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard/tree/main/samples/theshed)
- [The LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7518039721311232000/)
- [TheYard on GitHub](https://github.com/SteveStout/TheYard)
